New record-breaking binary linear codes constructed from group codes

Cong Yu Affiliation: School of Mathematics Affiliation: Hefei University of Technology Affiliation: Hefei, Anhui, People’s Republic of China, 230009 Email: zyu6952@gmail.com    Shixin Zhu Affiliation: School of Mathematics Affiliation: Hefei University of Technology Affiliation: Hefei, Anhui, People’s Republic of China, 230009 Email: zhushixinmath@hfut.edu.cn    Hao Chen Affiliation: College of Information Science and Technology Affiliation: Jinan University Affiliation: Guangzhou, Guangdong, People’s Republic of China, 510632 Email: haochen@jnu.edu.cn    Yang Li Affiliation: School of Mathematics Affiliation: Hefei University of Technology Affiliation: Hefei, Anhui, People’s Republic of China, 230009 Email: yanglimath@163.com    Xiuyu Zhang Affiliation: School of Mathematics Affiliation: Hefei University of Technology Affiliation: Hefei, Anhui, People’s Republic of China, 230009 Email: xyzfuman@mail.hfut.edu.cn
Abstract

In this paper, we employ group rings and automorphism groups of binary linear codes to construct new record-breaking binary linear codes. We consider the semidirect product of abelian groups and cyclic groups and use these groups to construct linear codes. Finally, we obtain some linear codes which have better parameters than the code in [10]. All the calculation results and corresponding data are listed in the paper or posted online.

   

August 24, 2026

Keywords Binary linear code ⋅\cdot Group ring ⋅\cdot Automorphism group ⋅\cdot Record-breaking code.

1 Introduction

Let 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q} be the finite field with qq elements. A qq-ary [n,k,d][n,k,d] linear code 𝒞\mathcal{C} is a kk-dimensional subspace of 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, where dd is the minimum distance of 𝒞\mathcal{C}. For 𝐚=(a1,a2,…,an),𝐛=(b1,b2,…,bn)∈𝔽qn\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}),\mathbf{b}=(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, the ordinary inner-product is defined by [𝐚,𝐛]=∑i=1nai​bi[\mathbf{a},\mathbf{b}]=\sum_{i=1}^{n}a_{i}b_{i}. The dual code of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is defined by

𝒞⊥={𝐜∈𝔽qn∣[𝐱,𝐜]=0,∀𝐱∈𝒞}.\mathcal{C}^{\bot}=\left\{\mathbf{c}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}\mid[\mathbf{x},\mathbf{c}]=0,\forall\mathbf{x}\in\mathcal{C}\right\}.

Two linear codes 𝒞1\mathcal{C}_{1} and 𝒞2\mathcal{C}_{2} are permutation equivalent if there is a permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} such that 𝒞1=π⁡(𝒞2)\mathcal{C}_{1}=\pi(\mathcal{C}_{2}), where SnS_{n} is the symmetric group on nn letters and π⁡(𝒞)={π⁡(𝐜)∣𝐜∈𝒞}\pi(\mathcal{C})=\left\{\pi(\mathbf{c})\mid\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}\right\}. The permutation automorphism group of 𝒞\mathcal{C} is denoted by PAut​(𝒞)={π∈Sn∣π⁡(𝒞)=𝒞}\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C})=\left\{\pi\in S_{n}\mid\pi(\mathcal{C})=\mathcal{C}\right\}.

Lemma 1.1.

[14] Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a binary linear code. Then PAut⁡(𝒞)=PAut⁡(𝒞⊥)\mathrm{PAut}(\mathcal{C})=\mathrm{PAut}(\mathcal{C}^{\bot}).

For fixed length nn and dimension kk, finding the largest possible value of minimum distance dd is an open problem in coding theory. In [10], Grassl provides online code tables that contains linear codes with the best known parameters. However, there are gaps between the lower and upper bounds on the minimum distance in the code tables. Improving the lower bounds or narrowing the upper bounds is a meaningful work in coding theory. In recent years, many scholars have made great contribution on improving the lower bound on the minimum distance in the code tables. Since cyclic codes, quasi-cyclic codes and constacyclic codes have good algebraic structure, they were used to construct new linear codes, for details see [1],[2],[3],[6],[5],[7],[20].
Group rings are useful tools in constructing codes. In [13], Hurley proposed group ring matrix(or GG-matrix). Group codes are ideals in group rings. In [8], the authors used GG-matrix to study group codes. Since then, GG-matrix have been widely used to construct some interesting codes(see [9],[11],[12],[16],[19],[22],[23]). The code generated by GG-matrix is an interesting class of codes because the group GG is isomorphic to a subgroup of the automorphism group of the code. Linear codes with large automorphism groups can reduce the amount of computation for encoding and decoding(see [17],[21]). However, in [10], the order of automorphism groups of most linear codes is very small, generally not exceeding their code lengths, and some are even trivial. This is not practical in the process of encoding and decoding. The order of the automorphism group of a code generated by a GG-matrix is at least equal to the code length. Therefore, when constructing a linear code with a GG-matrix, we can obtain good parameters and at the same time ensure that the order of the automorphism group is at least nn, where nn is the code length. In [15], Huffman gave a method for decomposing a linear code by using an automorphism of the code. Using this idea we can decompose a linear code into a direct sum of two subcodes through an automorphism of the code. Furthermore, if the properties of the two subcodes are better, a new record-breaking code can be constructed by the well-known Construction X.
The paper is structured as follows: In Sec. 2, we give some basic concepts about group rings and GG-matrix. In Sec. 3, we study the GG-matrix of several classes of groups which are semidirect products of abelian groups and cyclic groups. In Sec. 4, we give the idea of using the automorphism of codes to construct new record-breaking linear codes. In Sec. 5, we give the final calculation results and list them in the table. In Sec. 6, we give some possible directions for future research.

2 Group ring and GG-matrix

Let G={g1,g2,…,gn}G=\left\{g_{1},g_{2},\dots,g_{n}\right\} be a finite group of order nn. A group code is an ideal of a group ring 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G, where 𝔽q​G={∑i=1nαgi​gi∣αi∈𝔽q}\mathbb{F}_{q}G=\left\{\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}\mid\alpha_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}\right\}. The addition in 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G is defined by

∑i=1nαgi​gi+∑i=1nβgi​gi=∑i=1n(αgi+βgi)​gi,\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}+\sum_{i=1}^{n}\beta_{g_{i}}g_{i}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}(\alpha_{g_{i}}+\beta_{g_{i}})g_{i},

and the product of two elements in 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G is given by:

(∑i=1nαgi​gi)​(∑j=1nβgj​gj)=∑i=1n(∑j=1nαgi​gj−1​βgj)​gi.\left(\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}\right)\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\beta_{g_{j}}g_{j}\right)=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\left(\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}g_{j}^{-1}}\beta_{g_{j}}\right)g_{i}.

The group ring matrix was first introduced in [13]. Let v=∑i=1nαgi​gi∈𝔽q​Gv=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G, there is a natural bijection Ψ\Psi from 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G to 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}:

Ψ⁡(v)=(αg1,αg2,…,αgn).\Psi(v)=(\alpha_{g_{1}},\alpha_{g_{2}},\dots,\alpha_{g_{n}}).

Thus, in the later content, we can regard an elements in 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G as a vector in 𝔽qn\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}. Define the map σG\sigma_{G} from 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G to Mn​(𝔽q)M_{n}\left(\mathbb{F}_{q}\right) to be

σG​(v)=(αg1−1​g1αg1−1​g2αg1−1​g3⋯αg1−1​gnαg2−1​g1αg2−1​g2αg2−1​g3⋯αg2−1​gn⋮⋮⋮⋮⋮αgn−1​g1αgn−1​g2αgn−1​g3⋯αgn−1​gn),\sigma_{G}(v)=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\alpha_{g_{1}^{-1}g_{1}}&\alpha_{g_{1}^{-1}g_{2}}&\alpha_{g_{1}^{-1}g_{3}}&\cdots&\alpha_{g_{1}^{-1}g_{n}}\\ \alpha_{g_{2}^{-1}g_{1}}&\alpha_{g_{2}^{-1}g_{2}}&\alpha_{g_{2}^{-1}g_{3}}&\cdots&\alpha_{g_{2}^{-1}g_{n}}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots&\vdots\\ \alpha_{g_{n}^{-1}g_{1}}&\alpha_{g_{n}^{-1}g_{2}}&\alpha_{g_{n}^{-1}g_{3}}&\cdots&\alpha_{g_{n}^{-1}g_{n}}\end{array}\right),

where Mn​(𝔽q)M_{n}(\mathbb{F}_{q}) is the set of all n×nn\times n matrix over 𝔽q\mathbb{F}_{q}. The matrix σG​(v)\sigma_{G}(v) is called a group ring matrix or GG-matrix. The code generated by the row space of σG​(v)\sigma_{G}(v) is denoted by C⁡(v)C(v). It is not difficult to verify that C⁡(v)C(v) is a left principal ideal of 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G.

([13]) σG\sigma_{G} is an injective ring homomorphism, i.e. for v1,v2∈𝔽q​Gv_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G, σG​(v1​v2)=σG​(v1)​σG​(v2)\sigma_{G}(v_{1}v_{2})=\sigma_{G}(v_{1})\sigma_{G}(v_{2}).

For an element v=∑i=1nαgi​gi∈𝔽q​Gv=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G, we denote v(s)=∑i=1nαgi​gisv^{(s)}=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}^{s}. Then

Lemma 2.2.

([8]) Let GG be a finite group of order nn. For an element v=∑i=1nαgi​gi∈𝔽q​Gv=\sum_{i=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{i}}g_{i}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G, we have that σG​(v(−1))=σG​(v)T\sigma_{G}(v^{(-1)})=\sigma_{G}(v)^{T}, where σG​(v)T\sigma_{G}(v)^{T} is the transpose of σG​(v)\sigma_{G}(v). Moreover, the group GG isomorphic to a subgroup of PAut⁡(C⁡(v))\mathrm{PAut}(C(v)).

3 Several classes of groups and their GG-matrix

Let us review the semidirect product of two groups. Semidirect products are direct products in which the componentwise operation is twisted by a group-on-group action. Given two groups AA and BB, let φ\varphi be a homomorphism from BB to Aut​(A)\text{Aut}(A), where Aut​(A)\text{Aut}(A) is the automorphism group of AA. The semidirect product A⋊φBA\rtimes_{\varphi}B with the multiplication is defined by

(a1,b1)​(a2,b2)=(a1​φ​(b1)​(a2),b1​b2)(a_{1},b_{1})(a_{2},b_{2})=(a_{1}\varphi(b_{1})(a_{2}),b_{1}b_{2})

for all a1,a2∈Aa_{1},a_{2}\in A and b1,b2∈Bb_{1},b_{2}\in B. Notice that when φ\varphi is a trivial homomorphism, then A⋊φBA\rtimes_{\varphi}B is the direct product A×BA\times B with componentwise multiplication.
Let 𝐚=(a1,a2,…,an)∈𝔽qn\mathbf{a}=(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n})\in\mathbb{F}_{q}^{n}, we call the matrix

A=(a1a2…anan−1a1…an−2…a2a3…a1)A=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&a_{2}&\dots&a_{n}\\ a_{n-1}&a_{1}&\dots&a_{n-2}\\ \vdots&\vdots&\dots&\vdots\\ a_{2}&a_{3}&\dots&a_{1}\end{pmatrix}

the circulant matrix generated by 𝐚\mathbf{a}, denoted by A=c​i​r​c​(𝐚)A=circ(\mathbf{a}). Similarly, we denote the block circulant matrix by C​i​r​c​(A1,A2,…,An)Circ(A_{1},A_{2},\dots,A_{n}), where AiA_{i} are matrices of the same type, 1≤i≤n1\leq i\leq n. We call an nn by nn matrix a λ\lambda-circulant matrix if each element of its row vector is the result of moving each element of the previous row vector λ\lambda position to the right, and we denote it by c​i​r​cλ​(a1,a2,…,an).circ_{\lambda}(a_{1},a_{2},\dots,a_{n}). For example,

c​i​r​c2​(a1,a2,a3,a4)=(a1a2a3a4a3a4a1a2a1a2a3a4a3a4a1a2).circ_{2}(a_{1},a_{2},a_{3},a_{4})=\begin{pmatrix}a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}&a_{4}\\ a_{3}&a_{4}&a_{1}&a_{2}\\ a_{1}&a_{2}&a_{3}&a_{4}\\ a_{3}&a_{4}&a_{1}&a_{2}\end{pmatrix}.

Let [a]n[a]_{n} denote the smallest positive integer a′a^{\prime} such that a≡a′modna\equiv a^{\prime}\mod n. Notice that when λ=1\lambda=1, the 1-circulant matrix is actually a circulant matrix and if [λ1]n=[λ2]n[\lambda_{1}]_{n}=[\lambda_{2}]_{n}, then c​i​r​cλ1​(𝐚)=c​i​r​cλ2​(𝐚)circ_{\lambda_{1}}({\bf a})=circ_{\lambda_{2}}({\bf a}). We define TnT_{n} as a cyclic shift operator on a vector of length nn, i.e. Tn​(b1,b2,…,bn)=(bn,b1,…,bn−1)T_{n}(b_{1},b_{2},\dots,b_{n})=(b_{n},b_{1},\dots,b_{n-1}), where bib_{i} can be either a vector or an element. Let CnC_{n} be the cyclic group of order nn. Next we study GG-matrix of several classes of groups.

4 The automorphism groups of C⁡(v)C(v)

In this section, we focus on the binary case. The automorphism group of a binary linear code is actually its permutation automorphism group. A permutation π∈Sn\pi\in S_{n} is called type pp-(c,f)(c,f) if it has cc cycles of length pp and ff fixed points in its decomposition. For example, let π=(1,2,3)​(4,5,6)∈S13\pi=(1,2,3)(4,5,6)\in S_{13}, then π\pi is of type 33-(2,7)(2,7).
Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a binary linear code of length nn. Assume that an automorphism π=Ω1Ω2⋯ΩcΩc+1⋯Ωc+f∈PAut(𝒞)\pi=\Omega_{1}\Omega_{2}\cdots\Omega_{c}\Omega_{c+1}\cdots\Omega_{c+f}\in\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}) is of type pp-(c,f)(c,f), where Ω1,…,Ωc\Omega_{1},\dots,\Omega_{c} are disjoint cycles of length pp and Ωc+1,⋯,Ωc+f\Omega_{c+1},\cdots,\Omega_{c+f} are the fixed points. Let

Fπ​(𝒞)={𝐜∈𝒞∣π⁡(𝐜)=𝐜}F_{\pi}(\mathcal{C})=\left\{\mathbf{c}\in\mathcal{C}\mid\pi(\mathbf{c})=\mathbf{c}\right\}

and

Eπ(𝒞)={𝐜=(c1,c2,…,cn)∈𝒞∣∑i∈Ωjci≡0mod2,1≤j≤c+f}.E_{\pi}(\mathcal{C})=\left\{\mathbf{c}=(c_{1},c_{2},\dots,c_{n})\in\mathcal{C}\mid\sum_{i\in\Omega_{j}}c_{i}\equiv 0\mod 2,1\leq j\leq c+f\right\}.\
Theorem 4.1.

([15]) With the notations above, if gcd⁡(p,2)=1\gcd(p,2)=1, then 𝒞=Fπ​(𝒞)⊕Eπ​(𝒞)\mathcal{C}=F_{\pi}(\mathcal{C})\oplus E_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}). Moreover, Fπ​(𝒞)F_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}) and Eπ​(𝒞)E_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}) are π\pi-invariant.

From Theorem 4.1 we know that for a given automorphism of a binary linear code, we can decompose this code into the direct sum form of two subcodes. Our main ideas for constructing linear codes with good parameters are as follows:

  1. 1.

    Find a code 𝒞\mathcal{C} whose parameters are the same as or better than the best-known code in [10] with an automorphism π\pi.

  2. 2.

    Decompose 𝒞\mathcal{C} into the direct sum form of two subcodes by Theorem 4.1.

  3. 3.

    If 𝒞\mathcal{C} has parameters [n,k,d][n,k,d] and Eπ​(𝒞)E_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}) has parameters [n,k−k′,d′>d][n,k-k^{\prime},d^{\prime}>d]. Let 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} be a code with parameters [n′,k′,d−d′][n^{\prime},k^{\prime},d-d^{\prime}], then by using Construction X, we can obtain a code with parameters [n+n′,k,d′][n+n^{\prime},k,d^{\prime}].

The key to the above steps is to find Eπ​(𝒞)E_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}) with the largest possible dimension and the minimum distance larger than the original code 𝒞\mathcal{C}. The automorphism groups of the best known linear codes in [10] most are either trivial or of very small order, and therefore do not apply to our ideas. From Lemma 2.2 we know that the order of PAut​(C​(v))\text{PAut}(C(v)) must be a multiple of |G|\lvert G\rvert for v∈𝔽q​Gv\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G. Thus, we can try to decompose group codes to get some good subcodes.

Theorem 4.2.

Let G={g1,g2,…,gn}G=\left\{g_{1},g_{2},\dots,g_{n}\right\} be a finite group of order nn and v∈𝔽q​Gv\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G. If |PAut⁡(C⁡(v))|=n\lvert\mathrm{PAut}(C(v))\rvert=n and π∈PAut⁡(C⁡(v))\pi\in\mathrm{PAut}(C(v)) is of type pp-(c,f),p≠1(c,f),p\neq 1 then f=0f=0. In other words, π\pi has no fixed points, where pp is the order of π\pi and n=p​cn=pc.

Proof.

|PAut​(𝒞​(v))|=n\lvert\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}(v))\rvert=n implies that PAut​(𝒞​(v))≅G\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}(v))\cong G. Let v=∑j=1nαgj​gj∈𝔽q​Gv=\sum_{j=1}^{n}\alpha_{g_{j}}g_{j}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G. Then PAut​(𝒞⁡(v))={πg1,…,πgn}\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}(v))=\left\{\pi_{g_{1}},\dots,\pi_{g_{n}}\right\}, where πgi​(Ψ⁡(v))=(αgi−1​g1,αgi−1​g2,…,αgi−1​gn)\pi_{g_{i}}(\Psi(v))=(\alpha_{g_{i}^{-1}g_{1}},\alpha_{g_{i}^{-1}g_{2}},\dots,\alpha_{g_{i}^{-1}g_{n}}). If πgi\pi_{g_{i}} has a fixed point then there is a jj such that πgi​(αgj)=αgj\pi_{g_{i}}(\alpha_{g_{j}})=\alpha_{g_{j}}. Then gi−1​gj=gjg_{i}^{-1}g_{j}=g_{j} which implies that gi=Id​(G)g_{i}={\text{Id}}(G), i.e. p=1p=1. This yields a contradiction and we finish the proof. ∎

From the definition of Eπ​(C​(v))E_{\pi}(C(v)) and Fπ​(C​(v))F_{\pi}(C(v)) we quickly draw the following conclusion:

Theorem 4.3.

Let GG be a finite group of order nn and π\pi be an automorphism of C⁡(v)C(v) of type p−(c,0)p-(c,0) for v∈𝔽2​Gv\in\mathbb{F}_{2}G. Then the dimension of Fπ​(C​(v))F_{\pi}(C(v)) is less than or equal to cc, the minimum distance of Fπ​(C​(v))F_{\pi}(C(v)) is a multiple of pp and the minimum distance of Eπ​(C​(v))E_{\pi}(C(v)) is even.

5 Computational results

In this section, we will search for binary linear codes with good parameters based on Sections 3 and 4. All the upcoming computational results were obtained by performing searches in the software package Magma([4]).
We use the computer to search for a suitable v∈𝔽2​Gsv\in\mathbb{F}_{2}G_{s} such that C⁡(v)C(v) is a linear code with new parameters. However, if we use linear search, the number of times we search will reach 2n2^{n}, where n=|Gs|n=\lvert G_{s}\rvert. The number of searches explodes exponentially as nn increases, so this is obviously not advisable. Thus we use random searches. Notice that if we choose different v1,v2∈𝔽2​Gsv_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{2}G_{s}, C⁡(v1)C(v_{1}) may be equal to C⁡(v2)C(v_{2}).

Theorem 5.1.

Let GG be a finite group of order nn and v1,v2∈𝔽q​Gv_{1},v_{2}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G, if v2v_{2} is invertible in 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G then C⁡(v1)=C⁡(v2​v1)C(v_{1})=C(v_{2}v_{1}).

Proof.

It is obvious that C⁡(v2​v1)⊂C⁡(v1)C(v_{2}v_{1})\subset C(v_{1}). Since v2v_{2} is invertible, then there exists v3∈𝔽q​Gv_{3}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G such that v3​v2=1v_{3}v_{2}=1. We have C⁡(v1)=C⁡(v3​v2​v1)⊂C⁡(v2​v1)C(v_{1})=C(v_{3}v_{2}v_{1})\subset C(v_{2}v_{1}), thus C⁡(v1)=C⁡(v2​v1)C(v_{1})=C(v_{2}v_{1}). ∎

From Theorem 5.1 we know that if a code C⁡(v)C(v) is with parameters [n,k,d][n,k,d], there are many v′∈𝔽q​Gv^{\prime}\in\mathbb{F}_{q}G such that C⁡(v)=C⁡(v′)C(v)=C(v^{\prime}). The number of v′v^{\prime} that satisfy this condition depends on the number of invertible elements in 𝔽q​G\mathbb{F}_{q}G. Therefore, it is feasible for us to adopt computer search. We list our findings in Table 1 and the values of viv_{i} are listed in Table 2. In Table 1, we write new record-breaking codes in bold. Further, we give the order of the permutation automorphism groups of these codes in the last column.

From Theorem 4.3 we know that if there exists a binary [n,k,d][n,k,d] linear code 𝒞\mathcal{C} with an automorphism π\pi of type pp-(c,0)(c,0), where dd is odd. Then the minimum distance of Fπ​(𝒞)F_{\pi}(\mathcal{C}) is greater than dd. Using this result we can construct the following linear code which has a larger minimum distance than the best known code [108,23,35]2[108,23,35]_{2} in [10].

Theorem 5.2.

There is a binary [108,23,36] linear code.

Proof.

Let G2=(C7×C5)⋊C3=⟨x,y,z∣x7=y5=z3=1,xz=x2,yz=y⟩G_{2}=(C_{7}\times C_{5})\rtimes C_{3}=\left\langle x,y,z\mid x^{7}=y^{5}=z^{3}=1,x^{z}=x^{2},y^{z}=y\right\rangle and v∈𝔽2​G2v\in\mathbb{F}_{2}G_{2}, where Ψ⁡(v)=(100010010011010111101101000111100110001110101100111000001111010101100011001100000111011100011100110111110)\Psi(v)=(100010010011010111101101000111100110001110101100111000\\ 001111010101100011001100000111011100011100110111110). According to Magma’s calculations, C​(v)⊥C(v)^{\bot} is a binary [105,23,33][105,23,33] linear code and its automorphism group is iosmorphic to G2G_{2}. We select any element π\pi of order 35 in PAut​(C​(v)⊥)\text{PAut}(C(v)^{\bot}), then Eπ​(C​(v)⊥)E_{\pi}(C(v)^{\bot}) is with parameters [105,22,36][105,22,36]. From Theorem 4.1, Eπ​(C​(v)⊥)E_{\pi}(C(v)^{\bot}) is a subcode of C​(v)⊥C(v)^{\bot}. Let 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime} be the best known binary [3,1,3][3,1,3] linear code. Then by using Construction X for C​(v)⊥C(v)^{\bot}, Eπ​(C​(v)⊥)E_{\pi}(C(v)^{\bot}) and 𝒞′\mathcal{C}^{\prime}, we can obtain a binary linear code 𝒞′′\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime} with parameters [108,23,36][108,23,36]. Moreover, |PAut​(𝒞′′)|=630\lvert\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime})\rvert=630. ∎

However, when the minimum distance of a binary linear code is even, the minimum distance of its subcode may also be larger than that of the original code. We have decomposed all the codes in Table 1 and we obtain the following new code:

Theorem 5.3.

There is a binary [108,29,32] linear code.

Proof.

Let π\pi be an any element of order 35 in PAut​(C​(v13)⊥)\text{PAut}(C(v_{13})^{\bot}). Then Eπ​(C​(v13)⊥)E_{\pi}(C(v_{13})^{\bot}) is with parameters [105,27,32][105,27,32]. From Theorem 4.1, Eπ​(C​(v13)⊥)E_{\pi}(C(v_{13})^{\bot}) is a subcode of C​(v13)⊥C(v_{13})^{\bot}. Moreover, |PAut​(𝒞′′)|=105\lvert\text{PAut}(\mathcal{C}^{\prime\prime})\rvert=105. ∎

In fact, some special groups can also be used to construct new record-breaking linear codes. Magma includes all groups of order up to 2000 excluding the groups of order 1024. We choose groups SmallGroup(108,9) and SmallGroup(120,5), then binary codes [108,16,42] and [120,31,34] can be obtained from above two groups. All of the generator matrices and related data in Theorem 5.2 and 5.3 are showed online at https://github.com/Yucong1234/New_binary_linear_codes.

Theorem 5.4.

([14]) Let 𝒞\mathcal{C} be a binary [n,k,d][n,k,d] code. Then we can construct an [n−1,k,d−1][n-1,k,d-1] code by puncturing, an [n−1,k−1,d][n-1,k-1,d] code by shortening and an [n+1,k,d′][n+1,k,d^{\prime}] code by extending, where d′=d+1d^{\prime}=d+1 if dd is odd else d′=dd^{\prime}=d.

Then from Theorem 5.2-5.4, Table 1 and the above two record-breaking codes, we can obtain more new codes. We list the results in Table 3. Notice that Pi​Sj​EkP^{i}S^{j}E^{k} indicates that a code is punctured by ii times, shortened by jj times and extended by kk times.

6 Conclusion

In this work, we employ GG-matrix to find new record-breaking binary linear codes, where GG is the semidirect product of an abelian group and a cyclic group. By puncturing, shortening and extending, we obtain a total of 77 new record-breaking binary linear codes. In this paper, we only consider the binary case. In fact, the GG-matrix can generate many record-breaking non-binary linear codes. In addition, due to the limitation of computing power, we only search for linear codes with lengths less than or equal to 120. Interested readers can try non-binary cases or larger code lengths.
